Site-specific nutrient management in rice in Eastern India using a modeling approach
D. K. Das Æ Debtanu Maiti Æ H. Pathak
Received: 3 October 2007 /Accepted: 12 August 2008 / Published online: 5 September 2008 © Springer Science+Business Media B.V. 2008
Abstract Rice is the staple food of about 50%of the world's population. Rice yields in many parts of south Asia, however, are declining due to conventional blanket and imbalanced use of fertilizers. Fertilizer application based on quantitative approaches such as simulation modeling can assist in improving yields and nutrient use efficiency in rice. Field experiments were conducted in 20 sites in Eastern India to assess the soil supply, requirement and internal efficiency of N, P, K and Zn in rice. The data were used to calibrate the Quantitative Evaluation of the Fertility of Tropical Soils (QUEFTS) model for site-specific, balanced fertilizer recommendations. The parameters of maximum accumulation (a) and dilution (d) of N (31, 87), P (192, 678), K (33, 81) and Zn (32488, 153125) in plants were developed, which can be used as the standard parameters in the QUEFTS model for rice. metadata.section: Site-specific nutrient management in rice in Eastern India using a modeling approach

chunks.text:
Introduction
Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the primary staple food of almost three billion people, that is, about 50% of the world's population. Globally about 154 million ha of rice is harvested annually with a production of about 618.4 million Mg (IRRI 2005). More than 90% of this is produced and consumed in Asia. India, with 43.7 million ha under rice, produces about 140 million Mg of rice annually (MAC 2007). Rice yields in many parts of south Asia, however, are declining (Ladha et al. 2003; Pathak et al. 2003a). This may be due to conventional blanket and injudicious use of fertilizer which not only reduces nutrient use efficiency but also causes nutrient imbalance in soil resulting in decreased crop yield (Ladha et al. 2005). Fertilizer application based on quantitative approaches such as simulation modeling, which takes into account soil nutrient supplying capacity, crop nutrient requirement, efficiency of nutrient in soil and plant, can assist in improving nutrient use efficiency and rice yields. Estimates of fertilizer requirement for rice have been made through field experiments at several researcher-managed sites (Tandon and Tandon 1995; Pathak et al. 2003b). However, these estimates can only partly be extrapolated to farmers' fields, because of much broader range of soil, climatic and management conditions prevailing in the farms. Therefore, an estimation of fertilizer requirement should be based on simulation modeling (empirical or mechanistic) approach, which include broader ranges of soil and plant parameters and would be applicable to larger areas.

Introduction
The Quantitative Evaluation of the Fertility of Tropical Soils (QUEFTS), an empirical model, has been successfully used for calculating fertilizer requirement for rice, wheat and maize in many countries in Asia and Africa. The model was developed by Janssen et al. (1990) and applied in Kenya and Surinam for estimating fertilizer requirement for maize. It was further evaluated by Smaling and Janssen (1993) for maize in Kenya and Witt et al. (1999) for rice in south Asia. Pathak et al. (2003b) used the model to develop fertilizer management strategies for wheat in India whereas Liu et al. (2006) used it for wheat and maize in China. The present investigation was undertaken to (i) estimate N, P, K and Zn requirements by rice, (ii) estimate N, P, K and Zn supplying capacity of soil and (iii) develop sitespecific nutrient management in rice, particularly in Eastern India.

Background of the QUEFTS model
The pivot of QUEFTS model is the relation between nutrient uptake and yield. When a nutrient is available in limited quantities as compared to other nutrients, it is diluted within the plant and its concentration attains the minimum. The ratio of yield and nutrient uptake has then its maximum value. On the contrary, when a nutrient is abundantly available it accumulates in the plant till its uptake reaches its maximum value and the ratio of yield and nutrient uptake its minimum value. The model considers the interactions of N, P and K in calculating nutrient supplying capacity and crop yield. It assumes that yield is a function of nutrient supply from soil and fertilizer, and yield is limited only by the supply of nutrient taking into account the climatic and cultivarspecific potential yield of a given site (Janssen et al. 1990). In the model distinction is made between potential supply of a nutrient from soil and its actual uptake by the crop. Potential supply from a soil is the maximum quantity of a nutrient, which can be taken up by a crop. Actual uptake of a nutrient equals potential supply when other growth conditions are optimal. The QUEFTS calculates crop yield as a function of nutrient supply in four steps. In the first step, it assesses potential indigenous nutrient supply (INS) i.e., soil's supplying capacity of N (SN), P (SP) and K (SK). This can be done with estimation from soil chemical tests or from nutrient uptake in nutrient omission plots, a plot without application of the respective nutrient (Dobermann and White 1998; Witt et al. 1999). In the second step, the model calculates actual uptake of N (UN), P (UP), and K (UK) as fractions of potential supply of a nutrient (SN, SP and SK) i.e., INS plus actual supply of a nutrient applied through fertilizer taking fertilizer recovery efficiency (RE) into account. The third step in QUEFTS comprises of designation of yield ranges as functions of actual uptakes of N, P and K wh
en they are maximally accumulated (constant 'a') and maximally diluted (constant 'd'). The highest ratio of yield and nutrient uptake is taken as 'a' and the lowest ratio as 'd'.

Background of the QUEFTS model
Thus a given nutrient uptake value would result in two yield estimates, one for the situation where the nutrient is maximally accumulated and the other where the nutrient is maximally diluted (Janssen et al. 1990). The fourth step is calculation of the final yield by combining the yield ranges calculated in step three by accounting for the interactions between N, P and K (Janssen et al. 1990). The optimal nutrition could then be obtained by maximizing the total yield producing uptake efficiency as reported by Janssen et al. (1992). The uptake of a particular nutrient is assumed to be the most efficient in a situation of low supply of that nutrient as long as other nutrients are not limiting. As it is not possible to maximize the uptake efficiencies of all nutrients at a time, the mean of the N, P and K uptake efficiencies can be maximized (Janssen et al. 1992). The details of the model are given by Janssen et al. (1990, 1992) and some of the assumptions in the model and their validity have been described by Witt et al. (1999).

Field experiments
Two field experiments were conducted during kharif (June to October) and rabi seasons (November to April) in 2001-2003. The first experiment (Experiment I) was conducted for the determination of maximum accumulation 'a' and maximum dilution 'd' values, required for the parameterization and calibration of the model. The calibrated model was validated using the data from literature. The second experiment (Experiment II) was conducted for developing a site specific nutrient management (SSNM) strategy in rice using the validated model. All the experimental sites were located at 22°57 0 N latitude and 88°20 0 E longitude at an altitude of 7.8 m above mean sea level, about 130 km north of Bay of Bengal. The locations have a humid subtropical climatic condition. During kharif seasons of 20012002 and 2002-2003, total rainfall were 955 and 840 mm, average maximum temperatures were 32.6°C and 32.9°C and minimum temperatures were 25.5°C and 24.8°C. During rabi season of 2001-2002 and 2002-2003 the corresponding values were 39 and 142 mm, 29.3°C and 28.2°C, and 15.8°C and 16.4°C. The data were collected from nearest Meteorological Department of Bidhan Chandra Krishi Viswavidyalaya in Nadia district of West Bengal.

Field experiment I
The experiment was conducted by growing rice (cultivar IET 4094) at 20 farmers' fields during kharif in 2001-2002. The soils of the experimental sites had pH 6.8-7.7, organic C 4.1-5.6 g kg -1 and available N 469.4-542.3 kg ha -1 , P 9.5-18.8 kg ha -1 , K 59.0-102.5 kg ha -1 and Zn 0.9-1.4 kg ha -1 . The experiment was in a randomized block design with four replications. There were seven treatments: T1, N omission (-N ? PKZn); T2, P omission
(-P ? NKZn); T3, K omission (-K ? NPZn); T4, Zn omission (-Zn ? NPK); T5, balanced nutrition (? NPKZn); T6, control (no NPKZn). The N, P, K, and Zn were applied at 60, 30, 30, and 0.5 kg ha -1 , respectively. Irrigation was applied to maintain a 4-cm depth of standing water until 15 days before harvesting. Weeds, insects and diseases were controlled as required. At maturity, rice was harvested manually at 5 cm above ground level. The grains were threshed, dried, and weighed. Grain moisture was determined immediately after weighing. Grain yield of rice was reported at 14% moisture content. Straw weight was determined after oven-drying at 70°C to constant weight.

The highest and lowest internal efficiencies of the data set were taken as 'a' and 'd' values of QUEFTS, respectively. We excluded 5% of the highest and lowest values of the internal efficiencies to remove the outliers (set I, Table 1). To assess the sensitivity of the constants 'a' and 'd', another two sets of were derived by excluding 7.5 and 10% of the highest and lowest values of the internal nutrient efficiencies (sets II and III, Table 1). The model was run with each set of values with the supply of N, P and K as non-limiting and the potential yield of 7 Mg ha -1 .
Indigenous N supply (SN) was estimated from T1 treatment (N omission), whereas indigenous supplies of P (SP), K (SK) and Zn (SZn) were estimated from T2 (P omission), T3 (K omission) and T4 (Zn omission) treatments, respectively. The indigenous supplies of nutrients were plotted against the most common soil test methods i.e., soil organic C content, Olsen P, ammonium acetate-extractable K and DTPA-extractable Zn to develop relationships between INS and soil chemical test values. We also developed the relationships between grain yields in the respective nutrient-omission plots and nutrient uptake i.e., INS. These relationships can be used to estimate of INS from the grain yield data (Cassman et al. 1996; Dobermann and White 1999).

Field experiment II
Four field experiments on rice (cultivar IET 4094) were conducted during rabi (November to April), 2002-2003 in the farmers' field at block Ranaghat II, district Nadia, West Bengal to develop SSNM in rice. Fertilizer doses of N, P and K in each treatment were fixed using the validated QUEFTS model by putting 'a' and 'd' values of N, P and K of sets I, II and III (Table 1) for achieving the target yields of 5 and 6 Mg ha -1 . The following six treatments were employed in the study with four replications. T1: 'a' and 'd' values of set I, target yield of 5 Mg ha -1 ; T2: 'a' and 'd' values of set I, target yield of 6 Mg ha -1 ; T3: 'a' and 'd' values of set II, target yield of 5 Mg ha -1 ; T4: 'a' and 'd' values of set II, target yield of 6 Mg ha -1 ; T5: 'a' and 'd' values of set III, target yield of 5 Mg ha -1 and T6: 'a' and 'd' values of set III, target yield of 6 Mg ha -1 . On the basis of QUEFTS, N, P and K uptake were calculated for all sets of 'a' and 'd' values to achieve the target yield of 5 and 6 Mg ha -1 . The calculated N, P and K uptake were compared with their corresponding observed values.

Analysis of soil and plant samples
Soil samples were analyzed for organic C by Walkley and Black method (Page et al. 1982), available N by Kjeldahl method (Page et al. 1982), P by Olsen method (Olsen et al. 1954), K by neutral N ammonium acetate extraction method (Page et al. 1982) and Zn by DTPA-extraction method (Lindsay and Norvell 1978). Soil pH and electrical conductivity (EC) were determined in 1:2 soil-water ratio.
Plant samples were analyzed for N by Kjeldahl distillation as described by Jackson (1973) after digesting the samples with diacid mixture (H2SO4: HClO4 :: 9:1), and P and K by Vanado molybdate blue color and flame photometric methods, respectively, (Page et al. 1982) after digesting the samples with ternary acid mixture (HNO3:HClO4:H2SO4 :: 10:4:1). Zinc content was determined with the help of an atomic absorption spectrophotometer after digesting the samples with ternary acid mixture (HNO3: HClO4:H2SO4 :: 10:4:1).
Data analysis
The data were statistically analyzed for Duncan's Multiple Range Test (DMRT), correlation and multiple regression following the procedures outlined by Gomez and Gomez (1976).

Results and discussion
Yield and internal efficiency, requirement and recovery efficiency of N, P, K and Zn in rice
Grain yield in various treatments in farmers' fields ranged from 2.04 to 5.40 Mg ha -1 with N application rates varying from 0 to 60 kg ha -1 across the sites (Table 2). Total above-ground N accumulation ranged from 24.4 to 160.6 kg ha -1 and an internal efficiency of 29-88 kg grain kg -1 N with an average of 59 kg grain kg -1 N. Data showed that to produce 1 Mg of grain, the N requirement varied between 11.4 and 34.5 kg with an average of 16.9 kg (Table 2). Recovery efficiency of N (RN) varied between 31.2 and 42.3% (Table 2) with an average of 36.7%. Recovery of applied N varied considerably with amount of N applied.
Grain yield of rice in the experiments with P ranged from 2.46 to 5.38 Mg ha -1 , with application of P varying between 0 and 30 kg ha -1 (Table 2). Above-ground P accumulation ranged from 4.3 to 26.7 kg ha -1 . Internal efficiency of P ranged from 189 to 682 kg kg -1 , with a mean of 367 kg kg -1 . To produce 1 Mg of rice grain 1.9-4.5 kg P (mean 3.1 kg P) was needed. Recovery of P (RP) varied from 11.5 to 22.0% with a mean of 15.4% (Table 2).

Sensitivity of QUEFTS to 'a' and 'd' values
The sensitivity of 'a' and 'd' values was tested using three sets of the values (Table 1). Nutrient requirements calculated by the model were similar for all three sets of constants, except at yield levels that were close to the yield potential (Fig. 3). Such yield levels, however, rarely occur in farmer's fields. Thus, we propose to use the QUEFTS model parameters of set I (31 and 87 kg grain kg -1 N, 192 and 678 kg grain kg -1 P and 33 and 81 kg grain kg -1 K) for a standard version of QUEFTS focusing on decisionmaking on fertilizer requirements of rice, as this set of values include the maximum range of variability. Witt et al. (1999) estimated the minimum and maximum internal efficiencies (IEs) at 42 and 96 kg grain kg -1 N, 206 and 622 kg grain kg -1 P and 36 and 115 kg grain kg -1 K for QUEFTS. Their study was undertaken under diversified crop growing conditions (soil, climate, irrigation, variety) whereas the experimental sites of the current study were located in Eastern India where crop growing conditions are almost similar with respect to climate, soil, irrigation and variety.

Sensitivity of QUEFTS to 'a' and 'd' values
The model calculates nutrient requirements to achieve a specific yield target for different levels of potential yield. Depending on seasons and sites, the potential yield of currently grown rice in Eastern India ranges from 5 to 8 Mg ha -1 (Aggarwal and Talukdar and Mall 2000). The relationship between grain yield and nutrient accumulation of N, P and K as predicted by QUEFTS was linear at lower yield levels, reflecting a situation where plant growth was mainly limited by nutrient supply (Fig. 4). The model also calculates a decrease in internal efficiencies when target yields are close to potential yield. Thus, it may be more profitable for farmers to maximize nutrient efficiencies by a more balanced nutrition than to aim for higher yield targets with yield levels approaching maximum yields (Witt et al. 1999; Liu et al. 2006).
Fig. 4 Yields of rice in relation to nutrient uptake at 5, 6, 7 and 8 Mg ha -1 potential yields. The upper and lower lines indicate yields with maximum accumulation and maximum dilution of nutrients, respectively
Fig. 5 Yields of rice predicted by the QUEFTS model and observed in different locations in India
Regardless of yield potential the N:P:K ratios for 1 Mg grain in plants for the linear part of the relationship (up to 80% potential yield) was 6.5:1.0:6.8 as calculated by QUEFTS (Fig. 4). To produce 1 Mg grain 17.6, 2.7 and 18.3 kg N, P and K, respectively, would be needed. Witt et al. (1999) calculated requirement of 14.7 kg N, 2.6 kg P and 14.5 kg K (N:P:K = 5.65:1.00:5.58) for producing 1 Mg of grain until yield targets reached at 70-80% of potential yield.

Preliminary validation of the model
Four field experiments conducted by Singh et al. (1999); Swarup and Yaduvanshi (2000); Chandra et al. (2001); Katyal et al. (2001) at different locations of India were used to validate the calibrated QUEFTS model. Data from these experiments were not used for calibrating the model. The experimental sites differed widely in terms of climatic conditions and soil characteristics. For all experimental sites the observed yields were in good agreement with the predicted yields (Fig. 5) indicating that the model can be used to improve fertilizer recommendations for rice under diversified growing conditions. In earlier studies (Smaling and Janssen 1993; Witt et al. 1999; Pathak et al. 2003b; Liu et al. 2006) also the calibrated model yielded consistent results that were close to the observed ones.
Site-specific nutrient management in rice
The highest grain yield (5.83 Mg ha -1 ) was observed in the treatment T4 where NPK was applied at 64:51:50 kg ha -1 to achieve the target yield of 6 Mg ha -1 (Table 4). Irrespective of treatments 92-97% of predicted grain yield (based on QUEFTS) was in agreement with observed yield which indicates QUEFTS model can be used efficiently for prediction of grain yield and fertilizer recommendation in farmer's field. The highest uptakes of N (52.5 kg ha -1 ) P (14.6 kg ha -1 ) and K (109.2 kg ha -1 ) were observed in treatment T4 where NPK was applied based on QUEFTS at 64:51:50 kg ha -1 followed by T2[T6[T3 C T1 C T5. The observed N, P and K uptake were close (85-95%) to their corresponding predicted values. Sharma and Singh (2000) also suggested that fertilizer recommendations based on targeted yield concept were more balanced, profitable and helpful in controlling soil nutrient mining and was essential for sustainable crop production. Maiti et al. (2006) also reported that observed yields with different amounts of N, P, K, and Zn were in good agreement with the predicted amount of fertilizer nutrients in w
heat.
